note.note:
History:
- Presenting complaint: acute difficulty breathing and localized rash after an insect sting (bee/wasp) a few minutes prior to consultation.
- Onset/duration/progression: sting occurred "just a few minutes ago"; symptoms started immediately and are not reported to be progressing at time of consult.
- Associated symptoms: localized redness/blotchy rash and puncture mark on right arm; patient reports lips may be slightly swollen and "tongue feels a bit weird" (patient concern). Patient reports mild anxiety about symptoms.
- Context/triggers/previous episodes: insect sting (patient unable to distinguish bee vs wasp). No prior history of anaphylaxis or EpiPen use per patient.

Past Medical History:
- Eczema (patient-reported).
- Allergies: penicillin.
- Psychiatric: occasional anxiety/panic attacks; no history of pharmacologic treatment for anxiety.
- Medications: none reported / no regular medications documented.
- Past hospitalizations: none documented.
- Social: lives alone; has a cat; works as a computer scientist.

Physical Examination:
- General: alert, speaking normally; breathing not labored during video assessment.
- Airway/oral: mouth/throat exam performed — no visible throat or lip swelling; no stridor observed.
- Skin (right arm): puncture mark at sting site with slight redness and blotchy rash; described as a bit sore; no significant surrounding swelling noted.
- Other relevant negatives: no evidence of systemic anaphylaxis at time of exam (no respiratory compromise, no widespread urticaria reported).

Impression:
- Localized allergic/inflammatory reaction to insect sting (bee/wasp). No evidence of life-threatening anaphylaxis at time of assessment.

Management Plan:
- Immediate treatment advised: start an over-the-counter oral antihistamine.
  - Chlorphenamine (Piriton) recommended: 4 mg, one tablet, up to six times daily (as advised by clinician).
  - Alternative: a once-daily OTC antihistamine also suggested (specific agent/dose not documented).
- Safety advice: seek urgent care/ED immediately if any signs of deterioration — especially lip/throat swelling, increased difficulty breathing, stridor, or rapidly progressive symptoms.
- Infection advice: if redness spreads, becomes hot, or there are signs of local infection, clinician advised consideration of antibiotics and to re-present for assessment.
- Additional advice: no routine allergy testing currently indicated; consider allergy testing/blood tests only if reactions recur.
- Resources: clinician to provide information link about anaphylactic reactions for patient education.

Patient Summary:
- Patient sustained an insect sting minutes before consultation with a localized red, blotchy rash and puncture mark on the right arm and transient concern about lip/tongue sensation. Clinician assessed airway and breathing as stable with no evidence of anaphylaxis. Patient advised to take an OTC antihistamine and to seek emergency care if symptoms worsen.

Key Takeaways:
- Take an OTC antihistamine (chlorphenamine 4 mg as advised) to reduce the allergic response.
- Monitor closely for any breathing difficulty, throat/lip swelling, stridor, or rapidly worsening symptoms — go to the ED immediately if these occur.
- Return for review or contact clinician if rash spreads, becomes hot, or signs of infection develop.

Next Steps:
- Patient to obtain and initiate OTC antihistamine immediately.
- Patient to present to ED urgently if any airway/respiratory symptoms develop or if systemic signs appear.
- Reassess in primary care or via the service if rash persists, worsens, or if similar reactions recur (consider allergy testing if reactions become recurrent).

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: current vital signs (pulse, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, blood pressure, temperature) not documented; exact time of sting not precisely timed beyond "a few minutes ago"; comprehensive medication list and medication doses (other than suggested antihistamine) not documented; tetanus immunization status not documented; decision regarding EpiPen prescribing not documented.
- Internal conflicts from transcript: patient states age "twenty seven years old" and separately states birth year "1991, seventeenth of November" — these conflict (age vs DOB); conflict noted.
- Transcript quality: conversation largely clear and audible with occasional hesitations; visual inspection of rash/throat performed via video and documented by clinician.
